newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Railways joins crowd on Eurobond tracks.
newsitem.headline: Russian Railways joins crowd on Eurobond tracks.

text.p: The Russian Railways Ministry intends to follow in the tracks of the government and issue a Eurobond in 1997, the minister said on Tuesday, joining a host of firms and municipalities building up steam for Euroissues.
Minister Anatoly Zaitsev told reporters that the Ministry, with government guarantees, would begin issuing next year.

"There will be a trial issue of a few hundred million dollars. Our further actions will depend on the reaction of the market. It could be up to $2 billion a year," he said, adding the Finance Ministry and Central Bank had to approve the issue.
Russia is conducting a roadshow for its first Eurobond, likely to be issued late this month, which is expected to become a benchmark for Russian debt.

Analysts said the railways bond could succeed if Russia guaranteed it, but said a number of obstacles, such as foreign borrowing limits in the 1997 budget now being debated, could stop the plan on which Zaitsev said work has already started.
"There is certainly an appetite for sovereign East European debt," said Christopher Granville, head of research at United City Bank.
He said strong corporate issuers faced a good reception from foreign investors, as seen from the success of a recent issue of American Depositary Shares by natural gas monopoly RAO Gazprom.
But Troika Dialog fixed-income chief Robert Devane said that government guarantees came in a variety of forms and less than full backing would increase the spread the ministry must pay.
"Only if it is explicitly soverign backed is it just as good as the Eurobond coming out in a few days," he said.
The 1997 budget, which has not yet been passed, would cap Russian foreign borrowing at around 40 trillion roubles ($7 billion) for the year.
Granville said the ministry could be constrained by the limits but theoretically, would be able to hook up with the sovereign issue.
"If this pilot issue goes off well, Russia will issue $1-2 billion in next year. That could have a discrete issue dedicated for the railways," he said.
Even without a sovereign guarantee, the chugging state-owned monopoly, struggling with reorganisation, would be better off with Euro-borrowing, like many non-sovereign borrowers.
"A LUKoil Eurobond with the same maturity as the Russian sovereign, would pay about 250 basis points on the sovereign. It could not issue the same debt internally without a lot of pain," Devane said.
Analysts said that even if foreign investors' taste in Russian paper waned, further issues would not be derailed.

Moscow, St. Petersburg, Nizhny Novgorod and the Sverdlovsk region around Yekaterinburg as well as major firms including oil firm NK LUKoil and natural gas monopoly RAO Gazprom are considering Eurobond issues, which Devane said could add up to $10 billion next year.
"Even at very high spreads, you would be paying less than domestically," said Granville, who said Russian major oil companies were prime potential issuers.
"With the Eurobonds, it is not difficult to succeed."
